title: Not one stone (Mark 13:1–13)
hookLine: he foretells the temple's fall and hard times: don't be anxious what to say

cards: Picture a first-time visitor to a huge city, neck craned back, staring at the skyline. That's one of the disciples as they walk out of the temple.
In the King James Bible: "Master, see what manner of stones and what buildings are here!" King Herod had rebuilt the temple on a massive scale, and some of its stones were bigger than a truck.

Some of the giant stones of its outer wall still stand in Jerusalem today. Jesus says: "Seest thou these great buildings? there shall not be left one stone upon another, that shall not be thrown down."
Later they sit on the Mount of Olives, looking across the valley at the temple glowing in the sun, and four of them ask him quietly: when? And how will we know?

teach.b: What follows is the longest speech Jesus gives in Mark, all of chapter thirteen. Scholars sometimes call it the little apocalypse.
Christians read its strange images in several ways; it comes in three pieces, starting today. He gives them no date, just warnings. Watch out that no one deceives you.
Many will come claiming to be him. You'll hear of wars and rumors of wars; don't be troubled.
Earthquakes, famines: these are the beginnings of sorrows, a word for birth pains. Painful, but not the end. Then it gets personal.
You'll be handed over to councils, beaten, brought before governors and kings because of me. Families will split.

And right in the frightening part comes the most tender line: "take no thought beforehand what ye shall speak, neither do ye premeditate: but whatsoever shall be given you in that hour, that speak ye: for it is not ye that speak, but the Holy Ghost."
Don't lie awake scripting it. History adds a hard footnote.

teach.h: THE TEMPLE FELL IN THE YEAR 70.
teach.b: In the year 70, during a Jewish revolt, Roman armies destroyed the temple. It has never been rebuilt, and Jews mourn its loss to this day, especially on a fast called Tisha B'Av.

teach.h: IT IS NOT YE THAT SPEAK, BUT THE HOLY GHOST.
teach.b: Many scholars think Mark was written close to that time. The section ends: he that shall endure unto the end, the same shall be saved. Not the one with the best speech.

how: Christians facing trials or hard conversations often pray for the Holy Spirit's help in what to say, taking comfort from this promise, and many churches read Mark 13 in Advent.

games.q: what's inside the passage — tap the pairs.

s: Jesus gave the disciples a date
he gave warnings, not a date.
wars and earthquakes are called the end

the temple was destroyed by Roman armies in 70

games.q: you're told you'll one day stand before governors and kings because of your faith. what does Jesus tell you to do?
o: don't worry beforehand; say what is given you.
games.why: "take no thought beforehand what ye shall speak ... for it is not ye that speak, but the Holy Ghost."

practice: What conversation or moment are you already rehearsing in your head: the awkward talk, the interview, the appointment?
Picture setting it down like a heavy bag at the door; it'll still be there, but you don't have to carry it right now. If you pray, you can hand it to God and trust what will be given in that hour.

wordCard.voice: Little apocalypse: what scholars call Jesus's long speech of warnings in Mark chapter thirteen. The temple's stones would fall; in hard times, don't worry beforehand what to say.

orig.note: Greek: worry beforehand. pro, ahead, and merimnaō, to be anxious.

carryVoice: Your line: don't worry beforehand. The words will come in that hour. Day two hundred fifteen, done.
